claims.source: In contrast to the myofiber compaction defect of yorkie knock-down muscles, expression of an activated form of Yorkie (yorkie-CA), which cannot be phosphorylated by Warts, results in premature muscle fiber compaction already at 24 hr APF and strongly hyper-compacted muscle fibers at 32 hr APF, and later in disorganised myofibers (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claims.claim: Knock-down of hippo and warts results in premature muscle fiber compaction at 24 hr APF and hyper-compacted muscle fibers at 32 hr APF.
claims.source: Importantly, we observed the same phenotypes after knock-down of each of the two kinases hippo and warts, both negative regulators of Yorkie nuclear entry (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claims.claim: Dlg5, Slmap, hippo, warts, yorkie and scalloped are all expressed in developing flight muscles.
claims.source: Consistently, a transcriptomics time-course of dissected developing flight muscles (Spletter et al., 2018) showed that Dlg5, Slmap, hippo, warts, yorkie and also the transcriptional activator scalloped are all expressed in developing flight muscles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and a citation.

claims.claim: Expression of hippo[4A/431T] in muscle results in a muscle fiber compaction defect at 32 hr APF and muscle atrophy thereafter.
claims.source: Interestingly, expression of hippo[4A/431T] in muscle after Mef2-GAL4 driven flip-out also resulted in a muscle fiber compaction defect at 32 hr APF and muscle atrophy thereafter, phenocopying the STRIPAK and yorkie loss-of-function phenotypes (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Conditional activation of GAL4 only during pupal stages using temperature sensitive GAL80 does not affect myoblast fusion rates as measured by nuclei counts at 24 hr APF.
claims.source: Hence, we conditionally activated GAL4 only during pupal stages using temperature sensitive GAL80 (GAL80ts, see Materials and methods) (McGuire et al., 2003) and quantified myoblast fusion rates by counting the nuclei of DLM4. We found comparable numbers of nuclei at 24 hr APF ruling out a major contribution of myoblast proliferation or fusion defect to the phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B and a citation.

claims.claim: GAL80ts Mef2-GAL4 Dlg5 and yorkie knock-down muscles display the same fiber compaction defect as observed with Mef2-GAL4.
claims.source: Importantly, these GAL80ts Mef2-GAL4 Dlg5 and yorkie knock-down muscles do display the same fiber compaction defect as observed with Mef2-GAL4 resulting in longer but thinner fibers with grossly comparable volumes at 24 hr APF (yorkie-IR is slightly smaller) (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claims.claim: Conditional expression of yorkie-CA during pupal stages results in premature compaction at 24 hr APF and very short fibers at 32 hr APF that grow to disorganised fibers at 90 hr APF.
claims.source: Conversely, conditional expression of yorkie-CA during pupal stages results in premature compaction at 24 hr APF and very short fibers at 32 hr APF that grow to disorganised fibers at 90 hr APF (Figure 5A–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A–D.

claims.claim: Post-mitotic over-expression of hippo with Act88F-GAL4 results in flight muscle compaction defects at 32 hr APF and muscle atrophy at 48 hr APF.
claims.source: To further corroborate a post-mitotic role of the Hippo pathway in muscle fibers, we over-expressed hippo with the strong, strictly post-mitotic flight muscle specific driver Act88F-GAL4, which is only active after myoblast fusion (Bryantsev et al., 2012; Spletter et al., 2018). This post-mitotic over-expression of hippo resulted in flight muscle compaction defects at 32 hr APF and muscle atrophy at 48 hr APF (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E and citations.

claims.claim: Over-expression of Diap1 during pupal stages in GAL80ts yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down fibers substantially rescues fiber atrophy, often resulting in the normal number of six muscle fibers at 48 hr APF.
claims.source: Indeed, over-expression of Diap1 using UAS-Diap1 but not of a control construct (UAS-GFP-Gma) during pupal stages in GAL80ts Mef2-GAL4 (hereafter abbreviated as GAL80ts) yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down fibers substantially rescues fiber atrophy, often resulting in the normal number of six muscle fibers at 48 hr APF (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Over-expression of the exogenous apoptosis inhibitor p35 results in six muscle fibers at 48 hr APF in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles.
claims.source: Furthermore, over-expression of the exogenous apoptosis inhibitor p35 (Clem et al., 1991) also results in six muscle fibers at 48 hr APF (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C and a citation.

claims.claim: Apoptosis contributes to flight muscle fiber atrophy in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles.
claims.source: This demonstrates that apoptosis contributes to flight muscle fiber atrophy in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with Diap1 and p35.

claims.claim: GAL80ts Diap1-expressing yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down muscles fail to normally increase their cross-sectional area at 32 hr and 48 hr APF, resulting in smaller volumes at 48 hr APF.
claims.source: Interestingly, GAL80ts Diap1-expressing yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down muscles fail to normally increase their cross-sectional area at 32 hr and 48 hr APF, thus resulting in smaller volumes at 48 hr APF (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claims.claim: The Hippo pathway and its transcriptional co-activator Yorkie are required to enable normal post-mitotic growth of flight muscle fibers.
claims.source: Taken together, these data provide strong evidence that the Hippo pathway and its transcriptional co-activator Yorkie are required to enable normal post-mitotic growth of flight muscle fibers, likely by regulating the developmental timing of muscle morphogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the growth defects observed in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles even when apoptosis is inhibited.

claims.claim: GAL80ts Diap1-expressing yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down muscles fail to properly assemble their myofibrils at 32 hr APF resulting in only short myofibril traces.
claims.source: In contrast, GAL80ts Diap1-expressing yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down muscles fail to properly assemble their myofibrils at 32 hr APF resulting in only short myofibril traces (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: In yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles, nuclei form large centrally located clusters instead of being present mainly as single rows located between myofibril bundles.
claims.source: Concomitant with the myofibril assembly defect, we also found that the spacing of the nuclei is defective. In control muscle fibers the nuclei are present mainly as single rows located between myofibril bundles, whereas in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles they form large centrally located clusters (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: At 48 hr APF, the total number of myofibrils is strongly reduced in GAL80ts yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles compared to control.
claims.source: Furthermore, cryo cross-sections revealed that not only the cross-sectional area but also the total number of myofibrils is strongly reduced in GAL80ts yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles compared to control (Figure 7C,D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C,D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The Hippo pathway controls both the morphological quality of the myofibrils at the assembly and maturation stages as well as their quantity.
claims.source: As myofibril number is determined at the assembly stage at 32 hr APF in wild type (Spletter et al., 2018) these data demonstrate that the Hippo pathway controls both the morphological quality of the myofibrils at the assembly and maturation stages as well as their quantity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the myofibril defects observed in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Hypomorphic knock-down of the muscle attachment protein Kon-tiki (kon) results in a fiber compaction defect at 32 hr APF and a strongly reduced fiber cross-sectional area and volume at 48 hr APF.
claims.source: Upon hypomorphic knock-down of the muscle attachment protein Kon-tiki (kon), muscle-tendon attachment is compromised, hence mechanical tension build-up is perturbed and only fewer myofibrils can assemble (Weitkunat et al., 2014). Consistent with our results after yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down we find that kon knock-down also results in a fiber compaction defect, caused by reduced mechanical tension at 32 hr APF (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), and as a consequence in a strongly reduced fiber cross-sectional area and volume at 48 hr APF (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F and a citation.

claims.claim: Both mechanical tension and regulated Yorkie activity are required for normal myofibril morphogenesis to support muscle fiber growth.
claims.source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that both mechanical tension and regulated Yorkie activity are required for normal myofibril morphogenesis to support muscle fiber growth.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of kon knock-down and yorkie/Dlg5 knock-down phenotypes.

claims.claim: Over-expression of either Yorkie-CA or wild-type Yorkie post-mitotically using Act88F-GAL4 results in premature muscle fiber compaction at 24 hr APF.
claims.source: Over-expression of either Yorkie-CA, whose import into the nucleus is uncoupled from the Hippo pathway, or wild-type Yorkie, whose nuclear import is regulated by Hippo, both result in premature muscle fiber compaction at 24 hr APF, with seemingly normal actin filaments, phenocopying the Gal80ts condition (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: The muscle fiber hyper-compaction at 32 hr APF upon Yorkie over-expression coincides with a chaotic organisation of the myofibrils.
claims.source: Strikingly, the muscle fiber hyper-compaction at 32 hr APF coincides with a chaotic organisation of the myofibrils, with many myofibrils not running in parallel but in various directions (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Over-expression of a membrane-anchored myristoylated form of Yorkie does not result in premature muscle fiber compaction at 24 hr APF and displays normally oriented parallel myofibrils at 32 hr APF.
claims.source: In contrast, over-expression of a membrane-anchored myristoylated form of Yorkie, which has been shown to activate myosin contractility at the epithelial cell cortex without going into the nucleus (Xu et al., 2018), does not result in premature muscle fiber compaction at 24 hr APF. Furthermore, these muscles display normally oriented parallel myofibrils at 32 hr APF (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, and a citation.

claims.claim: The observed myofibril and fiber compaction defects are caused by a transcriptional response of Yorkie in the nucleus.
claims.source: These results indicate that the observed myofibril and fiber compaction defects are caused by a transcriptional response of Yorkie in the nucleus.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of nuclear and membrane-tethered Yorkie over-expression phenotypes.

claims.claim: Knock-down of scalloped results in severe muscle atrophy and no remaining muscles at 90 hr APF.
claims.source: This interpretation is corroborated by loss-of-function data of the transcriptional activator scalloped (sd), which is the essential transcriptional co-factor of Yorkie in the nucleus. Knock-down of scalloped results in severe muscle atrophy and no remaining muscles at 90 hr APF (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Expression of many core sarcomeric components is consistently reduced in yorkie 'loss-of-function' muscle genotypes (Dlg5-IR, Slmap-IR, and yorkie-IR) at 24 hr APF.
claims.source: Importantly, expression of many core sarcomeric components, including both titin homologs sallimus (sls) and bent (bt), Myosin heavy chain (Mhc), Myofilin (Mf), Paramyosin (Prm), tropomyosins (Tm1, Tm2), flight-muscle-specific actin (Act88F) and Obscurin (Unc-89), as well as sarcomere dynamics regulators, including myosin phosphatase (Mbs), a flight muscle formin (Fhos) and the spektraplakin shortstop (shot) are consistently reduced in yorkie 'loss-of-function' muscle genotypes at 24 hr APF (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Expression of mRNAs coding for proteins linking the nuclei to the cytoskeleton, such as the Nesprin family members klar and Msp300, are strongly reduced in yorkie 'loss-of-function' muscle genotypes at 24 hr APF.
claims.source: Furthermore, expression of mRNAs coding for proteins linking the nuclei to the cytoskeleton, such as the Nesprin family members klar and Msp300, are also strongly reduced (Figure 8B), which may explain the observed nuclei positioning defect in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 8B and inferred to explain the nuclei positioning defect.

claims.claim: Sarcomeric core components and their regulators are amongst the top upregulated genes in yorkie-CA and hippo-IR myofibers at 32 hr APF.
claims.source: Strikingly, sarcomeric core components and their regulators are amongst the top upregulated genes on both lists (Figure 8B, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 8B and Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: Genes important for myofibril attachment at muscle-tendon junctions, including the integrin attachment complex members kon, if, CAP, by, and Kank are upregulated in both yorkie-CA and hippo-IR genotypes at 32 hr APF.
claims.source: In addition to sarcomeric genes, genes important for myofibril attachment at muscle-tendon junctions, including the integrin attachment complex members kon, if, CAP, by, and Kank are upregulated in both gain-of-function genotypes (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: mRNAs coding for respiratory chain components are upregulated in hippo-IR and yorkie-CA myofibers at 32 hr APF.
claims.source: Consistently, we found an induction of mitochondria dynamics and protein import regulators (Opa1, Tom40) in hippo-IR and yorkie-CA myofibers at 32 hr APF as well as a consistent upregulation of mRNAs coding for respiratory chain components, including the F1F0 ATP synthase complex (complex V) subunit blw, the NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) subunit ND-75 and the Ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase subunit UQCR-C2, which are all required to boost ATP production during muscle fiber growth (Figure 8A,B, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 8A,B and Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: There is a mild reduction of Mhc and Act88F protein levels in yorkie knock-down muscles at 24 hr APF, which becomes more pronounced at 32 hr APF.
claims.source: Consistent with the transcriptomics data, we found a mild reduction of Mhc and Act88F protein levels in yorkie knock-down muscles at 24 hr APF, which became more pronounced at 32 hr APF (Figure 9A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by protein level quantification data shown in Figure 9A–C.

claims.claim: There is a reduction of Sls-GFP at 24 hr APF and a severe reduction of Prm-GFP at 32 hr APF in yorkie knock-down muscles.
claims.source: Furthermore, we have investigated protein levels for the myosin-binding protein Paramyosin (Prm) and the titin homolog Sls also using GFP fusion proteins. We found a reduction of Sls-GFP at 24 hr APF and a severe reduction of Prm-GFP at 32 hr APF in yorkie knock-down muscles (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by protein level quantification data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: Constitutive activation of yorkie (yorkie-CA) results in a boost of Mhc-GFP, Act88F-GFP, Sls-GFP, and Prm-GFP protein expression already at 24 hr APF, which is maintained at 32 hr APF.
claims.source: Surprisingly, constitutive activation of yorkie (yorkie-CA) results in a boost of Mhc-GFP, Act88F-GFP, Sls-GFP, and Prm-GFP protein expression already at 24 hr APF, which is maintained at 32 hr APF (Figure 9A–C, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by protein level quantification data shown in Figure 9A–C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: The increased acto-myosin and titin expression in yorkie-CA muscles may provide the molecular explanation of the premature compaction phenotype seen at 24 hr APF.
claims.source: This increased acto-myosin and titin expression may provide the molecular explanation of the premature compaction phenotype seen in yorkie-CA muscles at 24 hr APF.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between increased protein levels and premature compaction.

claims.claim: The Hippo pathway and its transcriptional regulator Yorkie contribute to the timing of myofibril assembly by regulating correct timing and levels of sarcomeric protein expression.
claims.source: Taken together, these data provide strong evidence that the Hippo pathway and its transcriptional regulator Yorkie contribute to the timing of myofibril assembly by regulating correct timing and levels of sarcomeric protein expression.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined transcriptomics and protein level data showing dysregulation in both loss and gain of function conditions.

claims.claim: Mammalian YAP1 can promote cardiomyocyte survival and growth, as post-mitotic deletion of YAP1 results in increased fibrosis and cardiomyocyte apoptosis.
claims.source: Interestingly, it was shown that mammalian YAP1 can promote cardiomyocyte survival and growth, as post-mitotic deletion of YAP1 results in increased fibrosis and cardiomyocyte apoptosis (Del Re et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Constitutive expression of active YAP in adult mouse muscle fibers induces muscle fiber atrophy and deterioration of muscle function.
claims.source: However, a role for the Hippo pathway in mammalian muscle is not limited to the heart. Constitutive expression of active YAP in adult mouse muscle fibers induces muscle fiber atrophy and deterioration of muscle function (Judson et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The mammalian Hippo homolog Mst1 is a key regulator in fast skeletal muscle atrophy.
claims.source: Furthermore, it has been shown that the mammalian Hippo homolog Mst1 is a key regulator in fast skeletal muscle atrophy (Wei et al., 2013), and more importantly YAP promotes muscle fiber growth by its transcriptional activity requiring Tead cofactors (Watt et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by citations.

claims.claim: YAP promotes muscle fiber growth by its transcriptional activity requiring Tead cofactors.
claims.source: Furthermore, it has been shown that the mammalian Hippo homolog Mst1 is a key regulator in fast skeletal muscle atrophy (Wei et al., 2013), and more importantly YAP promotes muscle fiber growth by its transcriptional activity requiring Tead cofactors (Watt et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The Hippo pathway via its transcriptional regulators Yorkie/YAP/TAZ is a general regulator of muscle fiber growth and survival in animals.
claims.source: This suggests that the Hippo pathway via its transcriptional regulators Yorkie/YAP/TAZ is a general regulator of muscle fiber growth and survival in animals.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of the pathway and similar phenotypes in flies and mammals.

claims.claim: Mammalian homologs Tead1-4 bind to a DNA motif called 'muscle CAT' (MCAT), a motif well-known to regulate cardiac skeletal sarcomeric protein expression.
claims.source: Interestingly, it has been shown that mammalian homologs Tead1-4 bind to a DNA motif called 'muscle CAT' (MCAT), a motif well-known to regulate cardiac skeletal sarcomeric protein expression, including cardiac Troponin T or cardiac actin (Carson et al., 1996; Farrance and Ordahl, 1996; Farrance et al., 1992; Wackerhage et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The only Drosophila Tead family member Scalloped binds to a very similar MCAT motif.
claims.source: The only Drosophila Tead family member Scalloped binds to a very similar MCAT motif (Wu et al., 2008), and we found loss of scalloped shows the same phenotype as loss-of-function of yorkie.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and corroborated by the phenotypic data.

claims.claim: Yorkie and Scalloped cooperate in Drosophila muscle to transcriptionally boost sarcomeric gene expression to enable myofibril assembly and flight muscle fiber growth.
claims.source: This strongly suggests that Yorkie and Scalloped cooperate in Drosophila muscle to transcriptionally boost sarcomeric gene expression to enable myofibril assembly and flight muscle fiber growth.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and transcriptomics data showing that both Yorkie and Scalloped are required for normal muscle development.

claims.claim: Flight muscle fate is determined by the zinc finger transcriptional regulator Spalt major.
claims.source: It has been shown that flight muscle fate is determined by the zinc finger transcriptional regulator Spalt major (Schönbauer et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Bruno is the major splice regulator of flight muscle alternative splicing of sarcomeric proteins, downstream of Spalt.
claims.source: One interesting link is that Yorkie and the Hippo pathway are required for the normal expression of bruno1 (bru1, see Figure 8B). Bruno is the major splice regulator of flight muscle alternative splicing of sarcomeric proteins, downstream of Spalt (Spletter et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and corroborated by the transcriptomics data.

claims.claim: Bruno binds to 3'-UTRs of mRNA to regulate their translation efficiencies.
claims.source: Additionally, Bruno was shown to bind to 3'-UTRs of mRNA to regulate their translation efficiencies (Webster et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Imp (IGF-II mRNA-binding protein) has been shown to regulate the stability and translation of a number of F-actin regulators.
claims.source: Another RNA-binding protein that requires the Hippo pathway for normal expression is Imp (IGF-II mRNA-binding protein, see Figure 8B). Imp has been shown to regulate the stability and translation of a number of F-actin regulators (Medioni et al., 2014), suggesting that post-transcriptional effects of Hippo signalling can play an important role, too.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and corroborated by the transcriptomics data.

claims.claim: Post-transcriptional effects of Hippo signalling can play an important role in muscle development.
claims.source: Imp has been shown to regulate the stability and translation of a number of F-actin regulators (Medioni et al., 2014), suggesting that post-transcriptional effects of Hippo signalling can play an important role, too.
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the regulation of RNA-binding proteins by the Hippo pathway.

claims.claim: Crosstalk between the Hippo pathway and translational regulation via the mTORC1 complex has been suggested in mammals.
claims.source: A similar crosstalk between the Hippo pathway and translational regulation via the mTORC1 complex has been suggested in mammals (Hansen et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Salvador, Expanded, Merlin, and Kibra, which regulate activity or plasma membrane localisation of Hippo in epithelial cells, all appear not to be required in flight muscles.
claims.source: Salvador, Expanded, Merlin, and Kibra, which regulate activity or plasma membrane localisation of Hippo in epithelial cells, all appear not to be required in flight muscles (Schnorrer et al., 2010; and data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is based on a citation and unpublished data.

claims.claim: Strip and Cka have been shown to bind to each other and regulate either Hippo or other signalling pathways in other Drosophila tissues including eye, testis or motor neurons.
claims.source: Interestingly, Strip and Cka have been shown to bind to each other and regulate either Hippo or other signalling pathways in other Drosophila tissues including eye, testis or motor neurons (La Marca et al., 2019; Neal et al., 2020; Neisch et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Slmap appears to be the specific adaptor to link STRIPAK to Hippo in muscle and epithelia in flies as well as in mammalian cell culture.
claims.source: Slmap appears to be the specific adaptor to link STRIPAK to Hippo in muscle (our work) and epithelia in flies (Neal et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2017) as well as in mammalian cell culture (Bae et al., 2017; Kwan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is based on the current study's data and supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Slmap has a single transmembrane domain and is likely localised to vesicles.
claims.source: As Slmap has a single transmembrane domain, it is likely localised to vesicles and our antibody stainings are consistent with at least a partial co-localisation to the assembling T-tubules, membrane invaginations that form during myofibrillogenesis and link the plasma membrane to the forming sarcomeres and the sarcoplasmic reticulum (Peterson and Krasnow, 2015; Razzaq et al., 2001; Sauerwald et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the protein structure and supported by immunostaining data and citations.

claims.claim: Dlg5 and Slmap were found in a complex with Mst1 (Hippo homolog) in mammalian cell culture.
claims.source: Slmap may either bind or recruit Dlg5 to membranes, both were interestingly found in a complex with Mst1 (Hippo homolog) in mammalian cell culture (Kwan et al., 2016), which may boost the interaction of STRIPAK with Hippo, resulting in its effective de-phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Mechanical tension produced by the actin cytoskeleton potentially via membranes, STRIPAK and Dlg5 may inhibit Hippo and thus promote the nuclear localisation of Yorkie.
claims.source: In analogy to the epithelial cell cortex, we hypothesise that mechanical stretch produced by the actin cytoskeleton potentially via membranes, STRIPAK and Dlg5 may inhibit Hippo and thus promote the nuclear localisation of Yorkie, which in turn will boost transcription of mRNAs coding for sarcomeric components.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their data and analogy to epithelial cells.

claims.claim: Filamentous actin (F-actin) levels can directly regulate Hippo pathway activity; more F-actin blocks Hippo signalling, resulting in epithelial tissue over-growth.
claims.source: Interestingly, it was shown that filamentous actin (F-actin) levels can directly regulate Hippo pathway activity; more F-actin blocks Hippo signalling, resulting in epithelial tissue over-growth (Fernández et al., 2011; Sansores-Garcia et al., 2011; Yin et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: A feedback loop may enable the induction of more actin and myosin once the myofibrils have started to assemble and produce high levels of mechanical tension.
claims.source: A similar feedback loop may enable the induction of more actin and myosin once the myofibrils have started to assemble and produce high levels of mechanical tension (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their data.

claims.claim: Only the successful completion of the myofibril assembly step allows to fully boost sarcomeric mRNA transcription and translation to enable myofibril maturation and muscle fiber growth.
claims.source: This feedback model implies that only the successful completion of the myofibril assembly step then allows to fully boost sarcomeric mRNA transcription and translation to enable myofibril maturation and muscle fiber growth.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the proposed feedback model and the temporal separation of myofibril assembly and maturation.

claims.claim: Mechanical control of the Hippo pathway and YAP/TAZ localisation by the actomyosin cytoskeleton is prominent in mammalian cells.
claims.source: Mechanical control of the Hippo pathway and YAP/TAZ localisation by the actomyosin cytoskeleton is also prominent in mammalian cells (Dupont et al., 2011; Wada et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: A mechanical feedback model may be a relevant mechanism to coordinate post-mitotic cardiomyocyte and skeletal muscle growth or regeneration in mammals.
claims.source: A similar mechanical feedback model as proposed here may therefore also be a relevant mechanism to coordinate post-mitotic cardiomyocyte and skeletal muscle growth or regeneration in mammals.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the conservation of the pathway and the proposed model.

results.result: Drosophila flight muscles undergo dramatic post-mitotic growth, increasing more than 10-fold in volume from 24 hr to 90 hr APF. At 24 hr APF, fibers are ~270 µm long with ~1000 µm² cross-sectional area; they compact to ~220 µm at 32 hr APF while assembling myofibrils, then grow to ~800 µm in length and ~4000 µm² cross-sectional area by 90 hr APF.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C26 provide quantitative measurements of muscle fiber dimensions at multiple developmental timepoints (24, 32, 48, 90 hr APF), supported by data in Figure 1A,C and Supplementary file 1. The measurements are internally consistent and establish the temporal dynamics of post-mitotic muscle growth.

results.result: Muscle-specific knockdown of Dlg5 or Slmap results in viable but flightless flies with complete flight muscle atrophy. At 24 hr APF, knockdown muscles are >20% longer than wild type and fail to compact at 32 hr APF, followed by complete atrophy by 48 hr APF. The phenotype is rescued by UAS-Dlg5-GFP but not control constructs.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C33 describe consistent phenotypes across multiple independent RNAi lines (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1). The rescue experiment (C30) provides genetic specificity. The temporal progression from compaction defect to atrophy is well-documented with quantitative measurements.

results.result: Dlg5 and Slmap proteins localize to T-tubule membranes at 90 hr APF, which are in intimate contact with myofibril A-bands. At earlier stages (32 and 48 hr APF), both proteins show partial co-localization with Dlg1 but display a more vesicular pattern compared to mature T-tubule markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2A-D with appropriate T-tubule markers (Dlg1, Amphiphysin). The temporal dynamics of localization from vesicular to T-tubule patterns are clearly documented. Citations support the T-tubule biology context.

results.result: Dlg5 interacts with STRIPAK complex components (Slmap, Fgop2, GckIII, Striatin/Cka, PP2A/Mts) in Drosophila muscle, with composition similar to mammals. Functional knockdown of STRIPAK members Cka and Strip phenocopies Dlg5/Slmap knockdown with compaction defects at 32 hr APF and subsequent muscle atrophy.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 are supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 3A,B, Supplementary file 1) identifying protein interactions, and genetic experiments (Figure 3D,E) showing similar phenotypes for multiple STRIPAK components. The conservation to mammals is supported by citations.

results.result: The Hippo pathway regulates developmental timing of muscle morphogenesis. Yorkie knockdown causes compaction failure at 32 hr APF and muscle atrophy, while yorkie-CA, hippo-IR, or warts-IR cause premature compaction at 24 hr APF and hyper-compaction at 32 hr APF. Expression of constitutively active hippo[4A/431T] (STRIPAK-binding deficient) phenocopies STRIPAK loss-of-function.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 demonstrate bidirectional genetic control with loss-of-function (yorkie-IR) and gain-of-function (yorkie-CA, hippo-IR, warts-IR) showing opposite phenotypes (Figure 4A,B). The hippo[4A/431T] experiment (C45, Figure 4C) provides molecular specificity linking STRIPAK to Hippo regulation. Transcriptomics data (C44, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) confirm expression.

results.result: The Hippo pathway functions post-mitotically in muscle fibers. Conditional GAL80ts experiments restricting knockdown to pupal stages show normal nuclei numbers at 24 hr APF but reproduce the compaction and atrophy phenotypes. Post-mitotic Act88F-GAL4 driven hippo overexpression also causes compaction defects and atrophy.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 use two independent temporal control strategies (GAL80ts and Act88F-GAL4) to demonstrate post-mitotic function. Nuclei counts (C46, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) rule out myoblast fusion defects. Phenotypes are reproduced with both systems (Figure 5A-E), providing strong evidence for post-mitotic function.

results.result: Apoptosis contributes to but does not fully explain muscle atrophy in yorkie/Dlg5 knockdown. Overexpression of apoptosis inhibitors (Diap1 or p35) rescues fiber number at 48 hr APF, but rescued muscles still fail to grow normally in cross-sectional area, resulting in smaller volumes. This demonstrates a growth-promoting role for Yorkie beyond apoptosis suppression.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 use genetic rescue with two independent apoptosis inhibitors (Diap1, p35) showing partial rescue (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C). Quantitative measurements (C53, Figure 6A-C) demonstrate persistent growth defects despite apoptosis inhibition, supporting a direct growth-regulatory role.

results.result: The Hippo pathway controls myofibril assembly quality and quantity. Yorkie/Dlg5 knockdown muscles (with Diap1) show short myofibril traces at 32 hr APF, defective nuclear positioning, and strongly reduced myofibril numbers at 48 hr APF. Knockdown of the tension-generating protein Kon-tiki produces similar compaction and growth defects, suggesting both mechanical tension and Yorkie activity are required for myofibrillogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 provide multiple lines of evidence: myofibril tracing (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), nuclear positioning (C56, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), and myofibril counting (C57, Figure 7C,D). The kon knockdown comparison (C59, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-F) provides mechanistic context linking tension to growth.

results.result: Yorkie functions as a transcriptional co-regulator in muscle nuclei. Post-mitotic overexpression of nuclear Yorkie (yorkie-CA or wild-type) causes premature compaction and chaotic myofibril organization, while membrane-tethered myr-Yorkie does not. Knockdown of the transcriptional co-factor scalloped phenocopies yorkie loss-of-function.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 use elegant genetic tools to distinguish nuclear vs. cytoplasmic Yorkie function. The membrane-tethered myr-Yorkie control (C63, Figure 7E) is critical for demonstrating nuclear requirement. Scalloped knockdown (C65, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B) confirms transcriptional mechanism.

results.result: The Hippo pathway controls sarcomeric and mitochondrial gene expression. In yorkie loss-of-function at 24 hr APF, core sarcomeric genes (sls, bt, Mhc, Prm, Act88F) and nuclear-cytoskeletal linkers (klar, Msp300) are downregulated. In yorkie gain-of-function at 32 hr APF, sarcomeric genes, muscle attachment genes (kon, if, CAP), and mitochondrial respiratory chain components are upregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 are supported by BRB-seq transcriptomics data (Figure 8A,B, Supplementary file 2) showing consistent changes across multiple genotypes. GO-term enrichment (Figure 8A, Supplementary file 3) confirms biological significance. The temporal specificity (24 hr for loss-of-function, 32 hr for gain-of-function) is appropriate for the developmental stages.

results.result: Yorkie regulates sarcomeric protein levels. Yorkie knockdown causes mild reduction of Mhc, Act88F, Sls, and Prm at 24 hr APF, becoming more pronounced at 32 hr APF. Yorkie-CA causes premature boost of these proteins at 24 hr APF, maintained at 32 hr APF, potentially explaining premature compaction. This demonstrates Yorkie controls timing and levels of sarcomeric protein expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 use GFP fusion proteins to quantify protein levels (Figure 9A-C, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-C), avoiding antibody variability. The temporal dynamics match transcriptomics data and phenotypes. The correlation between increased protein levels and premature compaction (C74) is logical but remains inferential.

results.result: The Hippo pathway is a conserved regulator of muscle fiber growth in animals. In mammals, YAP1 promotes cardiomyocyte survival and growth, while constitutive YAP activation causes muscle atrophy. Mst1 regulates skeletal muscle atrophy, and YAP promotes muscle growth via Tead-dependent transcription. This conservation suggests a general role for Yorkie/YAP/TAZ in muscle fiber growth and survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 summarize established mammalian literature with appropriate citations. The inference of conservation (C80) is reasonable given the molecular conservation and similar phenotypes across species, though it remains a hypothesis requiring direct testing in mammals.

results.result: Yorkie likely cooperates with Scalloped to regulate sarcomeric gene expression via MCAT motifs, potentially coordinating with the muscle fate determinant Spalt. Yorkie regulates RNA-binding proteins Bruno and Imp, suggesting post-transcriptional regulation may also contribute. Crosstalk with mTORC1 translational regulation has been suggested in mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C89 integrate literature on Tead/MCAT binding (C81-C82), Spalt function (C84), and RNA-binding proteins (C85-C87). While the transcriptomics data show Bruno and Imp are regulated by Yorkie (C85, C87, Figure 8B), the mechanistic connections remain speculative (C88, C89). Direct evidence for Yorkie-Scalloped cooperation on specific sarcomeric promoters is lacking.

results.result: STRIPAK regulation of Hippo in muscle differs from epithelia. Salvador, Expanded, Merlin, and Kibra are not required in flight muscles. Slmap appears to be the specific adaptor linking STRIPAK to Hippo in muscle, with a transmembrane domain suggesting vesicular/T-tubule localization. Dlg5 and Slmap were found in complex with Mst1 in mammalian cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are supported by negative genetic data (C90), literature on STRIPAK components (C91), and the current study's interaction data (C92). The localization inference (C93) is reasonable given protein structure and immunostaining. The mammalian Mst1 interaction (C94) is from published work.

results.result: A speculative model proposes mechanical tension from actin cytoskeleton inhibits Hippo via membranes/STRIPAK/Dlg5, promoting Yorkie nuclear entry and sarcomeric gene transcription. This creates a feedback loop where myofibril assembly generates tension that induces more actin/myosin expression, coordinating myofibril morphogenesis with transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 present a speculative mechanistic model (Figure 10) integrating the study's findings with literature on F-actin regulation of Hippo (C96). While the model is logical and consistent with the data, it lacks direct experimental evidence for the proposed mechanical-to-transcriptional signaling axis. The feedback loop (C97-C98) is an attractive hypothesis but remains untested.

results.result: Mechanical control of Hippo/YAP by actomyosin is prominent in mammalian cells, suggesting the proposed feedback model may be relevant for coordinating post-mitotic cardiomyocyte and skeletal muscle growth or regeneration in mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 extrapolate from the Drosophila findings to mammals based on pathway conservation and published mammalian mechanotransduction studies (C99). While the speculation is reasonable, it remains untested and would require direct experimental validation in mammalian muscle systems.
